claims.text: Equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni typically has an as-synthesized, predominantly FCC microstructure with minor BCC or disordered regions.
Moderately increasing Al content promotes local chemical ordering in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
Increasing Al content induces atomic-scale distortions.
Moderate Al enrichment shifts phase equilibrium from FCC toward BCC or a partially ordered phase.
In FeCoNiAl-based alloys, increasing Ni content increases the relative intensity of FCC diffraction peaks.
A controlled increase in BCC or ordered-phase fraction can optimize the combined high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
Above a critical Al concentration, excessive ordering causes brittle intermetallic phases to form.
The brittle intermetallic phases formed at high Al content degrade cryogenic toughness.
Al electronic effects modify the local bonding environment and phase energetics.
Atomic-size mismatch can produce lattice distortion that affects defect activity and mechanical properties in high-entropy alloys.
Al–Cr–Co–Fe–Ni exhibits chemical clustering or short-range ordering over portions of the investigated Al-composition and temperature ranges.
The proposed ordered state enhances high-temperature strength through increased lattice stability.
The proposed ordered state enhances environmental or oxidation resistance.
Within a favorable Al-composition window, the ordered state maintains radiation tolerance.
Within a favorable Al-composition window, the ordered state maintains cryogenic toughness.
Moderately Al-enriched samples will show increased BCC or partially ordered phase fraction by X-ray diffraction relative to the baseline.
Moderately Al-enriched samples will have improved high-temperature mechanical performance and oxidation resistance without reduced cryogenic toughness.
High Al levels will produce an abrupt appearance of brittle intermetallic phases accompanied by toughness loss.
The types and amounts of alloying elements influence the phases and properties of high-entropy alloys.
The equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni baseline has limited chemical ordering.

contradictions.description: The baseline is repeatedly called equiatomic, which implies about 20 at.% of each of the five elements, but it is also described as 'low-Al' or having 'minimal Al.' Those descriptions are compositionally inconsistent unless 'low' is explicitly defined only relative to Al-enriched comparison alloys.
